strengths: The core idea is useful and reasonably original: natural-language feedback is translated into pairwise labels, while Gaussian-process surrogates and standard BO acquisition functions retain a structured optimization loop.

The method is presented clearly through pseudocode, prompts, diagrams, and example conversations. The distinction between feedback acquisition, LLM labeling, surrogate fitting, and candidate generation is easy to follow.

The empirical study spans eight synthetic or simulator-based environments, uses 30 replications, reports uncertainty intervals, and includes useful ablations on scalar versus pairwise estimation, pair selection, feedback batch size, prior knowledge, LLM choice, and baseline acquisition functions.

The results consistently show strong early-iteration performance relative to the tested preferential-BO and LLM-only baselines, suggesting that globally informative feedback can improve optimization in feedback-limited settings.
The discussion acknowledges important limitations involving LLM interpretation errors, model-induced priors, and the absence of evaluation with actual human decision makers.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence relies entirely on an LLM-simulated decision maker, instantiated with the same Llama-3.3-70B model used by LILO in the main experiments. This creates a serious shared-model and communication-style confound: the interpreter may be unusually effective at decoding feedback generated by itself. Testing other interpreter models while retaining the same simulator does not resolve this issue, and there is no human study or evaluation across independently generated feedback styles.

The comparison does not control information or computational budgets. LILO receives globally descriptive natural-language answers and then makes K=64 pairwise-labeling queries with five LLM samples per pair in every iteration, whereas preferential BO receives only two pairwise judgments and true-utility BO only two scalar observations. Several initial messages also reveal exact targets, thresholds, directionality, or multiplicative structure. Consequently, the experiments demonstrate an advantage under substantially richer information, but do not isolate whether adaptive natural-language elicitation or the proposed surrogate construction is responsible.

Claims that LILO maintains calibrated uncertainty, principled exploration, and BO convergence properties are unsupported. A PairwiseGP fitted to correlated LLM-generated pseudo-labels does not automatically provide calibrated epistemic uncertainty, particularly when repeated completions are treated as observations. No calibration, label-accuracy, regret, or convergence analysis is supplied.

The simulated DM is prompted with ground-truth utility values for all observed outcomes and a textual utility description. This is much more internally consistent and quantitatively informed than typical human feedback. Robustness to inconsistent answers, preference drift, ambiguity, prompt injection, or noisy and partially articulated preferences is not evaluated.

There are material reproducibility problems. No code or artifact statement is provided; decoding parameters, random seeds, empirical normalization bounds, complete simulator constraints, and several optimization details are missing. Moreover, Algorithm 3 requests 64 distinct outcome pairs even in the first iteration, when batches of size d provide fewer than 64 possible pairs, without specifying replacement or another fallback.

The manuscript contains contradictory benchmark specifications: the main text describes DTLZ2 with d=4 and k=8, while the appendix uses d=8 and k=4; Car Cab Design is described as having nine outcomes in the main text but its appendix parameters and domain description use eleven. These inconsistencies impede faithful reproduction.

The practical significance is therefore not yet established. The real-world-labeled tasks are deterministic simulators, and no actual decision maker or expensive experimental system is studied. The paper also only briefly treats risks from the model imposing its own preferences and does not examine privacy, autonomy, or harmful misinterpretation in high-stakes preference elicitation. Overall, the promising idea and extensive simulated results merit consideration, but the shared-LLM confound, unequal information budget, and unsupported uncertainty claims require substantial revision before the central conclusions are reliable.

strengths: Originality/significance: LILO offers a potentially useful interface for preference-based Bayesian optimization by translating flexible natural-language feedback into pairwise labels for Gaussian-process utility models. The separation between language interpretation and BO is sensible and practically motivated.

Soundness: The paper evaluates several outcome/utility combinations over 30 replications and includes useful ablations of scalar versus pairwise estimation, pair-selection strategies, feedback batch size, priors, acquisition functions, and LLM backbones.

Presentation: The overall loop is easy to understand, figures communicate the main empirical trends clearly, and the appendix provides pseudocode, prompts, utility definitions, and example conversations.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges possible LLM-induced preference bias, imperfect interpretation of nuanced feedback, and the need to evaluate actual human decision makers.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central human-in-the-loop claim is not validated with humans. Every decision maker is another LLM whose prompt explicitly contains the ground-truth utility values, per-outcome contributions, and a textual description of the true utility. This creates an unusually informed synthetic oracle and does not establish that real users can provide equally consistent or informative feedback.

Soundness/fairness: The headline comparison does not control the information budget. LILO receives long, adaptively generated answers that can describe thresholds, directions, relative importance, and global utility structure, whereas preferential BO receives only two noiseless binary comparisons and true-utility BO only two scalar observations per round. Its superiority therefore does not isolate the proposed modeling method or demonstrate greater sample efficiency under comparable feedback cost.

Soundness: Using Llama-3.3-70B both as the main LILO agent and as the feedback simulator risks strong self-consistency or model-model communication effects. Testing alternative optimizer models while retaining the same simulator does not remove this concern. There is no evaluation across human annotators, independently designed simulators, ambiguous preferences, inconsistent answers, or adversarial feedback.

Soundness: Claims that the GP layer supplies calibrated uncertainty and reliable, principled behavior are unsupported. The paper reports neither predictive calibration or coverage nor regret/convergence analysis. Default PairwiseGP uncertainty fitted to correlated LLM-generated labels is not automatically calibrated uncertainty about the actual decision maker.

Reproducibility: Algorithm 3 always requests K=64 distinct outcome pairs, but the first batch provides fewer than 64 possible pairs in every reported environment (for example, 8 observations yield only 28 pairs). The stated random-sampling procedure is therefore undefined unless replacement or a smaller effective K is used. Other important LLM settings, failure/retry handling, and complete GP/acquisition optimization details are also absent, and no code artifact is identified.

Presentation/reproducibility: Benchmark specifications contradict one another. The main text states DTLZ2 has d=4 and k=8, although the appendix and experiments use d=8 and k=4; Car Cab is described with k=9 in the main text but its utility and prior messages contain 11 outcomes. These are material implementation ambiguities rather than cosmetic errors.

Significance/evidence: The manuscript calls simulator-based functions “real-world” problems and asserts successful application in multiple real-world online A/B-testing campaigns, but provides no campaign description, data, protocol, comparator, or result. Consequently, the practical deployment claim is unsupported.

Originality: The hybrid idea is promising but close to prior work on LLM-assisted BO and natural-language preference elicitation. The closest cited method, Austin et al. (2024), is not included as a baseline, making the incremental contribution difficult to quantify.

The evaluation covers only eight short, low-dimensional, deterministic optimization runs of eight rounds. It does not examine scalability, changing preferences, observation noise, long dialogue context, hallucinated interpretations, or whether LILO's 64 pairs times five LLM samples per round is competitive in monetary and latency cost.

Limitations/ethics: Although the paper candidly notes model bias and the absence of human evaluation, it does not address privacy of free-form preference transcripts, prompt injection or manipulation, disparate behavior across users and languages, environmental/API cost, or accountability in safety-relevant domains such as vehicle design. These omissions matter for the broad deployment framing.

strengths: Originality/significance: LILO is a useful and intuitive synthesis of natural-language preference elicitation, LLM-based preference translation, and GP Bayesian optimization. Separating linguistic interpretation from candidate selection is a sensible design that retains standard BO machinery.

Soundness: The evaluation covers eight outcome–utility environments, uses 30 replications with uncertainty intervals, and compares against oracle-utility, preferential-BO, and two LLM-only baselines. Ablations examine scalar versus pairwise labeling, pair selection, feedback batch size, prior knowledge, acquisition functions, and several LLMs.
The pairwise-labeling ablation provides an informative empirical result: translating language into comparisons appears more reliable than asking an LLM for absolute utilities.
Presentation: The method, algorithms, prompts, benchmark utilities, and representative conversations are extensively documented. Figures are legible and the main conceptual narrative is clear.

Limitations: The paper appropriately acknowledges dependence on LLM interpretation, possible contamination by model world knowledge, and the need to evaluate additional feedback sources, including humans.
weaknesses: Soundness: All decision-maker feedback is simulated by an LLM, and the same Llama-3.3-70B family is used for both the simulated decision maker and the main LILO agent. The simulator sees ground-truth utilities and their contributions. This creates a favorable self-play setting and does not establish that questions will elicit useful, consistent information from real users—the central target setting.

The principal comparison has an unequal information budget. LILO receives natural-language answers capable of revealing global thresholds, monotonicity, and tradeoffs, and then generates K=64 pairwise labels with five LLM samples per pair. Preferential BO receives only two ground-truth comparisons per iteration, while true-utility BO receives two scalar observations. Consequently, outperforming these baselines does not isolate the benefit of the proposed modeling method, and the sample-efficiency claim ignores substantial inference cost.

Claims that LILO maintains calibrated uncertainty and reliable BO behavior are unsupported: there is no calibration analysis, robustness study under systematically incorrect or contradictory feedback, or theoretical guarantee for the resulting nonstationary LLM-labeling process. Treating repeated LLM outputs as GP observations also does not by itself demonstrate calibrated predictive uncertainty.

Reproducibility has material inconsistencies. The main text specifies DTLZ2 with d=4 and k=8, whereas Appendix B gives d=8 and k=4; Appendix C likewise uses B_exp=d=8. Car Cab is described as having nine outcomes, but its piecewise-linear parameters and prior message contain eleven components. The L1 'utility' is described as a distance while optimization maximizes it, without specifying the transformation to [0,1]. The printed piecewise-linear formula also appears inconsistent with the stated diminishing-returns behavior and is discontinuous at the threshold as written.

Implementation information is incomplete for exact reproduction: there is no code artifact, random seeds, decoding parameters, serving/API configuration, empirical normalization bounds, or complete specification of some benchmark utilities. Default BoTorch settings and model names are insufficient given the sensitivity and cost of the many LLM calls.

Significance is presently limited by the short eight-iteration simulated studies and absence of actual human evaluation. The statement that LILO has been used in real-world online A/B campaigns is not supported by experiments, protocols, or results in the manuscript.

Originality is meaningful but moderate because the components—LLM preference elicitation, LLM-assisted BO, pairwise GP preference learning, EUBO, and LLM warm starts—are established. The contribution is primarily their integration, whose advantage is not cleanly separated from the richer feedback supplied to LILO.

Ethics and deployment limitations need fuller treatment. The paper mentions model-prior bias but does not analyze misleading questions, preference distortion, privacy of user feedback, unsafe optimization recommendations, or safeguards for high-stakes applications. Any claimed real-user deployment should also clarify consent and data governance.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically appealing hybrid: an LLM translates free-form feedback into pairwise labels, while a pairwise GP and standard acquisition functions retain the optimization machinery of preferential BO. This is a useful combination of existing ideas and the supporting-role design is more credible than treating an LLM as the optimizer.

The experimental suite is broad for a simulation study: ten structured environments, typically 16–32 replications, longer-horizon tests, and ablations over feedback budget, pairwise versus scalar elicitation, pair selection, acquisition function, priors, and LLM choice. The text-summarization study also begins to test the claimed applicability to unstructured outcomes.

The manuscript is generally well organized and supplies prompts, pseudocode, utility definitions, and baseline descriptions. It candidly acknowledges the absence of human studies and that quantitative-feedback baselines can catch up or surpass LILO at longer horizons.

The results consistently suggest that language can efficiently communicate global preference structure when such structure is accurately verbalized, and the reported pairwise-label accuracy provides a useful diagnostic of the proposed pipeline.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim about natural-language feedback from decision makers is not adequately supported because every main experiment uses an LLM simulator rather than humans. The simulator is given the ground-truth utility values and a textual description of the utility, and is explicitly instructed to align its answers with them. Moreover, both the simulator and the main LILO agent use Llama-3.3-70B. This creates a favorable machine-to-machine communication channel with shared linguistic biases; changing only the receiving model in one three-environment ablation does not address this dependence.

The comparison against quantitative feedback is fundamentally information-imbalanced. Initial language messages sometimes disclose exact target points, thresholds, monotonicities, and interaction structure, after which LILO generates up to K=64 pseudo-comparisons per trial. The quantitative baselines receive only Bpf local scalar values or comparisons. Thus, findings such as one message being equivalent to 8–16 oracle labels largely reflect how much oracle information was placed in that message, not a controlled comparison of human effort or feedback efficiency. No timing, cognitive-load, token, or information-budget study is provided.

The method is described as producing calibrated uncertainty, but no calibration experiment or theoretical justification is given. A GP posterior fitted to many correlated, deterministic labels generated by one LLM from the same feedback does not automatically yield calibrated epistemic uncertainty; treating those pseudo-labels through a standard pairwise likelihood does not establish the claim.

The so-called true-utility BO baseline is nonstandard and weaker than the name suggests: it observes utilities for only Bpf selected outcomes, fits a Y-to-utility GP, imputes utilities for all evaluated outcomes, and then fits another X-space GP. Consequently, the headline statement that LILO outperforms true-utility BO is potentially misleading. Comparisons to direct BO with utility for every evaluated configuration, and to stronger structured-language extraction or parametric-preference baselines, are needed.

The unstructured-text experiment also contains privileged information. Its simulated decision maker sees automatically computed indicators and the overall latent utility and is instructed to align with it, while the LILO pairwise judge receives the gold reference summary in addition to language feedback. This does not demonstrate optimization from a real decision maker's free-form feedback alone. The evaluation is also small—20 test articles—and the paper does not clearly report replication counts or uncertainty for this study.

Algorithm 2 has material specification problems. For S=4, its q=ceil(sqrt(2S)) rule gives q=3, which yields only three unordered pairs, fewer than S; the correct condition is q(q-1)/2 >= S. The pseudocode also stores comparisons as outcome tuples while fitting a proxy over X without explicitly retaining the corresponding input mapping, may exceed K when K is not divisible by S, and does not specify duplicate-pair handling. These ambiguities impede faithful implementation.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the extensive appendix. Both the abstract and reproducibility section contain an empty code link. Important details such as LLM serving configuration, decoding parameters, random-seed control, failure/retry behavior, computational and token costs, and the summarization model and data splits are missing. Reliance on default BoTorch settings is also too vague for a complex two-stage experimental pipeline.

The evidence is restricted to low-dimensional search spaces (mostly d <= 8) and synthetic, hand-designed utilities; the long-horizon results show the advantage diminishing or reversing. Accordingly, claims of compatibility with high-dimensional problems, real-world usefulness, and stable sample-efficient optimization are broader than the evidence supports.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the principal contribution combines LLM-based preference interpretation with established pairwise-GP BO and qEUBO. The paper offers no new inference or convergence analysis, and the related-work discussion does not experimentally establish advantages over the closest language-based preference-elicitation methods.

The impact statement is perfunctory. A system that interprets human preferences raises foreseeable concerns about misinterpretation, demographic and cultural bias, prompt manipulation, privacy of free-form feedback, and overconfidence in consequential optimization. These risks and appropriate human oversight are not discussed, although the limitations concerning simulated users are appropriately acknowledged.

strengths: Originality/significance: The combination of free-form language elicitation, LLM-based pairwise labeling, and a GP-based Bayesian optimization loop is intuitive and potentially useful. Positioning the LLM as an interpreter rather than the optimizer is a sensible design choice.

Soundness, within the simulated setting: The experiments cover ten outcome–utility environments, use 16–32 replications, and include useful ablations of labeling budget, pair selection, acquisition function, optimization horizon, prior knowledge, scalar versus pairwise estimation, and LLM choice.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and provides extensive pseudocode, prompts, utility definitions, and environment details. The distinction among experimental outcomes, latent utility, language feedback, and the proxy model is explained well.
The text-summarization experiment is a useful preliminary demonstration that the method can consume unstructured outcomes without explicitly modeling the outcome space.
weaknesses: Soundness—the central human-feedback claim is not validated: there is no study with human decision makers. In the main experiments, Llama-3.3-70B both simulates the DM and interprets the resulting feedback. The simulator is given the exact utility description, precomputed ground-truth utilities, and per-outcome utility contributions. This highly favorable model-to-model channel does not establish that real, noisy, inconsistent human language can be translated reliably enough for optimization.

The comparison underlying the headline claim that one language message is worth 8–16 oracle labels is not information- or effort-matched. Several hard-coded initial messages expose nearly the whole objective—for example, the L1 target point and the piecewise-linear thresholds—whereas the quantitative baselines receive only a few localized evaluations or comparisons. The observed advantage can therefore follow directly from supplying LILO substantially more global information, rather than from the proposed inference procedure.

The same-model simulator/judge setup risks strong self-consistency bias. Although the LLM ablation changes the interpreting model, the simulator remains Llama-3.3-70B, and the main result uses the identical model on both sides. Tests with humans, independently authored feedback, paraphrase/adversarial perturbations, contradictory or drifting preferences, and genuinely different simulator families are needed.

The paper repeatedly describes the GP uncertainty as calibrated, but provides no calibration evidence such as coverage, reliability, log predictive density, or comparison against the latent utility. A PairwiseGP posterior conditional on potentially systematic LLM labels is not automatically calibrated for the true decision maker.

Technical specification contains an apparent inconsistency: Algorithm 2 chooses q=ceil(sqrt(2S)) outcomes and then requests S distinct pairs, but q choose 2 can be smaller than S—for the reported S=4, q=3 yields only three pairs. Duplicate handling across labeling chunks and behavior when the available pair set is smaller than the requested sample are also unspecified.

Significance is overstated relative to the evidence. The summarization study still uses an LLM feedback agent explicitly shown numerical utility indicators and instructed to align with the oracle; it has only a four-dimensional search space and 20 held-out articles. It therefore does not substantiate broad claims about high-dimensional text or image outcomes in realistic decision-making.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code is available but displays no accessible location, and it does not report key LLM inference settings, computational/API cost, parsing and retry behavior, or sufficient execution details to reproduce stochastic model calls. Reliance on large hosted models further complicates exact replication.

Limitations and ethics are treated too lightly. The discussion acknowledges simulated feedback, but not the circularity and unequal-information comparison above. The impact statement does not address preference misinterpretation, model bias, privacy of user feedback, manipulation through generated questions, or safeguards for consequential optimization.

Overall, the framework is promising and the simulated engineering study is extensive, but the evidence does not support the central real-world and human-feedback claims. Corrected baselines and independent or human feedback evaluation would require substantial new experimentation rather than a minor revision.

strengths: Originality/significance: LILO offers a compelling integration of natural-language preference elicitation with preferential Bayesian optimization. Restricting the LLM to interpreting feedback while a GP surrogate handles uncertainty and acquisition is a useful, practically motivated design.

Soundness: The paper evaluates 10 outcome-utility environments with 32 replications in the main benchmark and generally reports confidence intervals. Results show strong early-stage performance, which is the regime most relevant when black-box evaluations are expensive.

The evaluation is unusually broad: it includes two LLM-only baselines, scalar- and preference-feedback BO baselines, longer horizons, feedback-budget studies, pairwise-versus-scalar labeling, pair-selection and acquisition-function ablations, alternative LLMs, prior-informed initialization, and a text-summarization case study.

The evidence helps isolate why the approach works: pairwise LLM labels are reported to reach approximately 85–90% accuracy, pairwise supervision outperforms direct scalar prediction, and qEUBO selection is beneficial when the labeling budget is small.

Presentation is clear and polished. The problem formulation, three-stage optimization loop, algorithms, prompts, simulator utilities, and baseline implementations are described in substantial detail; figures communicate the early-optimization advantage effectively.

The authors appropriately acknowledge that the advantage decreases over longer horizons, that quantitative-feedback methods can eventually catch up, that the experiments use simulated decision makers, and that the unstructured-outcome experiment is preliminary.
weaknesses: The central empirical limitation is the absence of evaluation with real human decision makers. The simulated DM is given the exact utility description, ground-truth utilities, and per-outcome utility contributions and is explicitly instructed to remain consistent with them. This creates a substantially cleaner preference channel than realistic human feedback, so the experiments do not establish robustness to ambiguity, inconsistency, preference drift, misunderstanding, or heterogeneous users.

The feedback-efficiency comparison is not fully controlled. LILO converts each natural-language response into as many as K=64 pairwise pseudo-labels per trial, whereas the quantitative baselines receive only Bpf=2 direct observations or comparisons. This can be reasonable if human interactions are the sole resource, but message length, response effort, LLM calls, tokens, latency, and monetary cost are not measured. LILO also elicits feedback before the main loop, making exact budget equivalence unclear. Consequently, claims that one language message is equivalent to 8–16 oracle labels should be presented more cautiously.

The repeated claim of “calibrated uncertainty” is unsupported. A PairwiseGP supplies posterior uncertainty, but training it on correlated, LLM-generated labels does not imply calibration. The paper reports neither predictive calibration nor coverage, and the model appears not to account explicitly for systematic LLM bias, dependence among labels generated from the same feedback, or uncertainty in the translation step.

There is a concrete inconsistency in Algorithm 2: choosing q=ceil(sqrt(2S)) does not guarantee S distinct pairs. For the stated S=4, q=3 yields only three unique pairs, although the algorithm subsequently assumes a batch of four. The correct minimum q must satisfy q(q-1)/2 >= S. This should be corrected and reconciled with the implementation.

Some headline conclusions are stronger than the results. In the main benchmark, LILO does not uniformly dominate at every environment and horizon; quantitative baselines catch up or surpass it in several longer runs. The summarization experiment only matches the strongest oracle-feedback baselines, uses a hand-crafted latent metric, and instructs the simulated DM to align with an exposed “overall_utility” indicator, making it a limited demonstration of genuinely unstructured subjective optimization.

Reproducibility is mixed. The appendix supplies extensive pseudocode, prompts, utility definitions, and model classes, but the manuscript’s code link is blank. Important operational details such as inference settings, decoding randomness, parsing/retry rules, exact BO optimization settings, random seeds, and a full accounting of LLM calls are not sufficiently specified.

The evaluation does not stress failure modes such as adversarial or contradictory feedback, distribution shifts in preferences, inaccurate textual priors, model-family mismatch between the DM and interpreter, or systematic label bias. The LLM ablation is limited to three DTLZ2 environments, while the same Llama family is used as both simulator and primary interpreter in the main study.

The generic impact statement is inadequate for a system intended to infer and optimize human preferences. Relevant concerns include sensitive preference data, demographic or cultural bias in LLM interpretation, manipulation or over-optimization of imperfectly inferred preferences, and unsafe outcomes caused by confident misinterpretation. These issues warrant explicit discussion and safeguards.
